This sexually dimorphic body size, where males substantially outweigh females, is linked to intrasexual competition for breeding access during the rut. Longevity records for the dromedary indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 28.4 years [am = approximately 28.4 years] under captive conditions at a core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], though free-ranging individuals rarely exceed 20 years due to predation, disease, and periodic droughts. Physiological studies suggest that the species' remarkable tolerance for hyperthermia and dehydration contributes to this longevity by reducing cumulative oxidative damage incurred during thermal stress events. Comparative analyses among camelids reveal that the dromedary's life span is intermediate between that of the smaller vicuña (about 15 years) and the larger Bactrian camel (which may reach 35 years in captivity), highlighting a positive allometric scaling of longevity with body mass within the family.

This rate is achieved only when females have access to abundant forage following favorable rainfall events; during prolonged droughts, reproductive output may cease entirely through embryonic resorption or anovulatory cycles. The weaning mass of approximately 253.5 kilograms [Wwx = approximately 253.5 kilograms] represents about 58 percent of the adult female's body mass, an exceptionally high relative weaning mass compared to other domestic livestock, and underscores the protracted maternal investment that defines the species' life history. The interplay between these life-history traits—low fecundity, late maturity, and extended parental care—positions the dromedary as a highly specialized survivor in one of the planet's most demanding terrestrial biomes.
